title: Ritual 1
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer suggests that our daily lives, including our meditation practice, are actually rituals that can help us connect with ourselves and the world on a deeper level. Rather than seeing these practices as a means to an end or a way to achieve some external goal, we should approach them as a way to cultivate awareness, inner peace, and compassion for ourselves and others. By embracing our daily rituals in this way, we can tap into a deeper reality and live more mindfully, bringing benefit not just to ourselves, but also to those around us.

sentences.text: I appreciate all the work that has gone into producing this retreat.
When I come to a retreat, I don't think about it in advance.
I'm lucky if I can get on the plane with my suitcase packed.

So I don't think about it at all, and then whenever I arrive I think, wow, look at all that everybody has had to do to make this happen: to create a whole world that didn't exist, to transform a space into a sacred space, to create an atmosphere in which things are possible that usually aren't possible, and perspectives suddenly become available to us that usually aren't available to us.
So I want to thank everybody who has put in all this work.
We know who they are, the usual suspects, who have really done a lot to make this happen with a lot of love and skill.
And maybe some of you are wondering, why does it have to be so complicated anyway?
Why do we have to do all of this stuff, all these details?
Maybe you think that meditation makes some sense, but do we really need the rest of it?
Do we need the chanting and the bowing?
Do we really need to stand in just this way and walk in just that way?
Do we need to eat like that?
Isn't this just some cultural form created in China or Japan a long time ago?
Most of us are not Chinese or Japanese, and even if we were, we all speak English and we were all born in the 20th century.
And really, even in China and Japan, do they still need to do all that?
One could wonder about these things.
Our culture has a very pragmatic, materialistic, and scientific view that more or less questions the validity of ritual.
We're interested in effective mechanisms, things that work.
Ritual seems like an extra overlay, like window dressing on top of that.
Maybe it's nice, but is it really necessary?
And then also, there are a lot of problems with ritual.
For one thing, if you're not used to it, and some of you in the retreat may not be used to it at all, or not too used to it, it seems foreign and alienating.
We all want to feel included, and ritual makes you feel like an outsider if you're not used to it.

Then all kinds of thoughts come into your mind as a result of that, and you could spend a lot of time dealing with all those thoughts that seem like they wouldn't be there if it weren't for this ritual.
Now of course, this particular aspect of ritual goes in both directions.

Once you get used to it, you feel really at home with it, and then you feel more included than you otherwise would, because you went through the initiatory phase of not being used to it, and now you're used to it.
So now practice can feel more intimate and more wonderful, exactly because you've passed through that gate, you've gotten used to it, it's taken time.
And now the ritual and the form seem particularly valuable to you, exactly because they brought you closer to one another, to the sangha members, and closer to your own heart.
So in that sense, ritual is good, but also bad.

It's good because now we have a group of very intimate Dharma friends who have a wonderful way of sharing practice together through these ritual forms, and it's also bad because now we have an in-group and a not-so-in-group.
Although I think that none of us looks at it that way, still something like that happens, and all the different thoughts and feelings that go along with it are unavoidable.
Even though none of us want that, I think none of us want that, and none of us like it, we can't help it.
The forms, the rituals, seem to produce those kinds of thoughts and feelings.
And then also, ritual has the problem, if you're not used to it, of causing you to feel like you're always making a mistake.

You thought before you came here that you knew how to walk, you knew how to stand, you knew how to sit, you knew how to eat, and now you find out that you could stand, walk, sit, eat, incorrectly, and need to be corrected, or feel like you're making a mistake about it.
Nobody likes to make mistakes.
When you make a mistake, you feel foolish and diminished, and then a whole other bunch of negative thoughts start kicking in.
So we could be really busy with a lot of thoughts just because of the ritual, and we could think, is it worth it?
And then there are even worse problems than that, because a lot of us, when we were children, practiced rituals of all sorts.
Maybe we practiced religious rituals, and at some point we became disappointed in the religion, or the people who were conveying it to us.
We felt like it was false, it wasn't what it was supposed to be, it wasn't what we thought it was when we were younger.
So we began to see all that ritual as being fake, and deceptive, and in some cases maybe even coercive.
Painful.

And then, as we got still older, and we talked to our friends, and we studied history, we found out that religion was so often the destructive force in history, that religion oppressed a lot of people, sometimes politically, taking away their money and their rights.
And sometimes, or in addition to that, psychically, taking away people's sense of autonomy and freedom, and we found that in our own case.
We saw that mirrored in what happened to us, all because of the coercive nature of ritual.
So we don't like ritual that much, and we want something beyond ritual.
Something more real, something more personal, more open, more relevant.
So we don't like ritual.
So, okay, they do it, so we'll do it, but we don't really like it.
Maybe this sounds familiar to you, you could relate to this.
I think this is very commonplace.
I think this is the way most of us see it.
And we come to it honestly, by what we study, what we thought, what has happened to us, by our whole point of view.
A couple of evenings ago, I was in Larkspur, California, which is like a lot of towns around San Francisco, a cute little town.
Like a lot of towns around San Francisco, a cute little town with a lot of good restaurants and gift shops.
And I was there, it was evening, and I was walking across the street.
I was with Kathy, my wife.
We were crossing the street, and there was pavement, and there was a sidewalk, some cars going by, and there was the curb, and there was a bright red traffic light on the other side of the street.
The lights of the little hotel and the restaurant that we were going into were lit up, and you could see the people sitting inside.
I'm sure that you've walked across a street just like that.
It was all very real to me, and it was all very substantial.
I was in Larkspur, but all of a sudden I could feel just how flimsy all this was.
It was so clear that underneath this little few inches of pavement was the earth.
I don't know how many thousands of miles of earth, with this tiny little, completely insignificant piece of pavement on top of it, as far as the sky reaches and out into space.
And it was so obvious that the pavement, the buildings, the traffic light were so temporary and vulnerable, perched there on the surface of the earth.

You could feel that the earth had been there a very, very long time before anybody ever dreamed of Larkspur, California, and put up a few little pieces of something that we call Larkspur, California, and that the earth would be there a long, long time when Larkspur was gone.
And this reality, this fact of the earth being there, was not a theory or a thought.
It was really a fact.
It was actually there.
You could feel yourself walking on the earth.
And it was very beautiful to feel that.
It kind of expanded my sense of where I was and my sense of wonder about what my life was.
Maybe you have experienced this too.
But most of the time, I'm not on the earth.
Most of the time, I'm not a dignified human being full of wonder.
I'm just myself on the way to Larkspur, or just leaving Larkspur.
And it makes me wonder, what am I really?
What is the most fundamental person that I am?
And where am I really?
What is the most fundamental place that I'm occupying at any time?

So what I'm trying to say is that all our ideas about who we are, what we want, what's good, what's bad, what meditation practice is, why we think we're trying to do it, what ritual is, why we think we don't like it: this is all the news that comes from Larkspur.
Larkspur comes from the surface of our lives.
And I'm not saying that Larkspur is not important.

If I was a resident of Larkspur and they were having an initiative on the ballot because they needed more taxes to fix up town hall, I would vote for it, because Larkspur is important and we need to take care of it.
So it's not that this is trivial.
It's just that Larkspur is depending on something more.
Even though we can't see it, and even though most of the time we don't think about it, we can't forget it.
So our whole retreat, our entire practice, is actually nothing but ritual.
The meditation practice is also ritual.
And it's ritual that evokes and touches us below the surface.
Of course, none of us think that way in the beginning.
We don't come here for the Zen Buddhist ritual.
Probably nobody, myself included, who has ever practiced Zen in the West has come for the lovely Zen Buddhist ritual.
We've all come for ourselves, for our lives, for our curiosity about reality, our human needs.
But after a while, it dawns on us that first it seems like our practice, and then we realize our whole life, actually isn't about us.
We thought our life was about us, but actually it turns out it's not about us.
And this dawns on us, or maybe comes to us suddenly.
We've all been given a life here, a life which nobody knows what it is or how it comes about.
We've been given life for a reason, each one of us.
And none of us knows exactly what the reason is.
And the life that is our life didn't just start with us.
Our life comes to us from the measureless past, through generations and generations, to come to us.
And now it's with us for a little while, and it will flow through us onward to new destinies we have no idea of.
So we're all living our own lives, but also each life is a living out of the destinies of the past, and is a preparation for the destinies of the future.
So we're not meditating to clarify our minds or improve our emotional or mental health.
We are immersing body and mind deeply in the way, as we chanted this morning, in order to redeem the whole of the past and to provide benefit for the whole of the future.
We added a few elements to morning service which we practice in the monastery, but I don't think we've ever done here before.
First we chant the verse of repentance:
*All my ancient twisted karma from beginningless greed, hate and delusion born through body, speech and mind.*
This is a profound verse, a verse of repentance and purification, in which we say, and from time to time we mean it.
A lot of times, like all rituals, the effort is always to bring your whole heart to a ritual, and it's always an effort because you never can do that except once in a while.

If you try to bring your heart and don't, there's a one time when your heart is there and is transformed by the ritual, and you realize that it was those other hundred times that kind of boosted you up to that.
So the one time when it means something to you, you realize that your chanting is saying: this is the karma of the past.
This whole catastrophe, all of it, I take it on, I own it, it's mine.
I accept this full human responsibility, and in doing so, in the act of doing so, I open up my heart and I open up my hand and I purify it.
I turn it around by accepting it.
I turn it around.
And in turning it around, in this moment, I and everyone with me begins life over again pure.
And then while we're pure, before we mess it up, we have a moment there when we're pure.
The first thing we do is take refuge in Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, so that we get some help, a boost.
Taking refuge means to return, to return home, to return to our real home, our true home what we really are most deeply, what's at the core, at the center of the Earth of our lives.
A Buddha, the nature of awakening, the human possibility to live with kindness and clarity that each one of us has by virtue of our human consciousness: we say I return to that.
The Dharma, the way of life that comes from kindness and love and harmony: we return to that.
The Sangha, the community of all being, to awakening, to love, to connection.

Out of gratitude for all that we are, out of gratitude for the fact that we're here, we're healthy, we're together in mutual support, in the beauty of our own bodies and of the Earth, out of that gratitude we make an offering of fragrant incense.
And they say that incense has always been offered in different traditions because the sense of smell and fragrance is closest to the invisible life.
So we offer that fragrance.
And we make prostrations, surrendering our whole body and mind.
We're bowing really to ourselves, with a wish that eventually we will be capable of completely giving ourselves to ourselves in this way, as Buddha, as awakening itself.

And then we chant sutras and intone magic spells to train our heart mind in the teachings, so that it's not just thinking about the teachings like the way we read a book but embodying the teachings with our voice, and with one voice, all of us together.
This trains our hearts.
And also generates virtue.
And then with this virtue that we've generated we can make more offerings.
We can offer not only the fragrance in our own body and heart, but we can offer the virtue produced by these chantings of sutras.
We can offer them in gratitude to the Buddhas and others who've brought teachings to us, and also offer them to those in need of healing.
So this is what we're doing in this ritual of service, which is strengthened by our sitting.
We're expressing our commitment to our highest human potential.
We're offering everything we have to that.
We're expressing our gratitude for this mysterious life that we've been given and our commitment to using it in the best way possible.
And we're offering the virtue of what we're doing for the benefit of others.
So I realize that you might not have thought about service in that way.
It's just words you chant and so forth.
But I think eventually we all feel this way about the service.
And none of this makes that much sense, I suppose, in terms of our Western scientific materialistic worldview.
But somehow in some other way it does make sense.
And we feel it, in a way that's so deep that it's not even quite right to say that we feel it, the same way we feel cold or hot or happy or sad.
There's some other kind of feeling that comes into our lives through the practice, through the service.
When I stand in front of the altar, as I did this morning, I try to orient myself to this wide and deep world of our practice.
I try to find within myself the person I am that is far more than the person I think I am.

And I try to enter completely that true person with my body and mind, and to enter the ritual in the spirit of that person, so as to make it effective and meaningful not only for myself and you but for the whole lineage of human beings.
All of us have always tried to understand what we are and why we're here, and have always been reaching for an ultimate meaning that goes beyond anything we could ever think or experience.

When we chant the words of the service and make these ritual gestures, I think we're joining not only the millions and millions of Zen Buddhists today and in the past who've done these rituals, but also all practitioners of Buddhism everywhere in Asia and the West who have engaged in rituals that come from the same root, and all human beings who have ever chanted or danced or prayed or made offerings or created ceremonies.
This is what human beings do.
This is what human beings have always done.
Wherever you go, anywhere in the world through the past, the earliest recorded past, you find people have always done this.

And when we do it we're joining with them, body through the breath, through the heart, with this beginningless and endless human hope to be in connection with one another, with the earth, with our highest possible goodness.
And this ritual heals us.
This is from the record of Zhaozhou.
*A monk asked, "In the days of the Buddha it was transmitted by the Buddha.
After Buddha passed into Nirvana, who is there to transmit it?"
The Master said, "The entirety of the past and present are in me."
The monk said, "It's not clear to me what was it that was transmitted?"
The Master said, "All things are subject to birth and death."
The monk asked, "So it's impossible to do away entirely with the Buddhas and ancestors?
What was it that was transmitted?"*
Transmission is a big word in Zen and in Buddhism.
And usually in Zen we say, there's nothing at all to transmit.
There is no teaching, there is no special secret that someone whispers in your ear.
There's nothing at all to the countless volumes of teachings.
It's the simplest thing in the world.
It's just life, really living our life.
But life at the center of the Earth.
Not just life in Larkspur.
And that's why we have to make some effort.
We have to pierce the pavement of Larkspur.
We don't have to stop being in Larkspur, we just have to see through the pavement.
So it takes some kind of effort.
And so we have this whole tradition of practice and the many traditions of practice, so that we can somehow with our whole body understand something, transmit something: that there's nothing to it.
So it is a kind of a joke, but it's a serious joke.
All things are subject to birth and death.
That's also a kind of a joke.
But it's a pretty serious joke.
So I don't know if it's a good idea for me to be telling you all this on the first day of sesshin.
Maybe it's a bad idea, but I didn't have much time.
This is the first thing that came into my mind, to get used to the schedule and somehow make more time.
And I certainly am not telling you all this so that you should all feel that you should have lofty motivations and deep feelings.
If you have lofty motivations and deep feelings, that's good.
I don't want to say no, but I'm just not trying to make you feel that you ought to.
If you have come to get a little more concentration and clarify your life and improve it, excellent.
I think it will help.
Don't worry about having more metaphysical and noble motivations.
Anyway, your motivations are noble and metaphysical, whether you know it or not.
And you'll find out eventually.
Every period of Zazen when you sit down, give your full respect to the spot on Earth where you're sitting.
This is a sacred place.
It's your spot.
No one else can sit there.
And you have to bring that spot to life.
So bow to the place and sit on it with that sort of intention and that sort of respect.
And then as you set your body on your cushion, finding a good balanced way of sitting and lifting up your body, it's not just your body.
It's the Buddha body.
It's the only Buddha body in that place.
So take care of it in that way as you sit with your full human dignity, lifting up from the inside.
Sometimes the Zazen posture we can feel as if it's imposed on us.
We're supposed to be sitting in such and such a way.
But it's the opposite.
It comes from inside of us.
So rather than feeling like when you sit down you're going to get your body in a posture, it's a strange way of thinking.
That's how we think.
But it's a strange thing, like there's somebody outside of you that's going to come and get your body into a certain posture from the outside.
But there is nobody, there's no you outside of, from the inside.
You let your body, in other words, you let go of all in your body that doesn't want to let you express your full human dignity.

You just let it go and allow the body to be uplifted, and feel how the back part of your head floats up toward the ceiling, and feel how your bottom part of your body is held by the Earth, and sit suspended there between the heavens and the center of the Earth, and let your body be held in that spot.
And as you bring your awareness to your body, you'll feel that.
So take your time to feel yourself sitting on your seat, and to allow the full expression of that sitting there to occur.
And then gently find your breathing.
And again, we're not trying to produce some kind of breathing.
We're just trying to find and release the breathing that's there, letting it be full and complete.
And you can think of it that way, a full breath, a complete breath.
All the way in, all the way out.

And if there's some way you're preventing that, if there's something in you that has been preventing a full and complete breath, completely accepting life when you breathe in, completely letting go of life when you breathe out, if there's something in you that hasn't been allowing that, see if you can let go and let the breathing be complete.
And then if you want to, a practice that you can experiment with is, when you breathe out, you can breathe out Buddha.
You can say softly in your mind Buddha, next breath Dharma, next breath Sangha, over and over like that.
And whatever else arises in the mind, be aware of it.
But come back with the breath to Buddha, Dharma, Sangha.
Or another way of doing the same thing is to concentrate your attention on your heart, complete generosity and openness that is the natural state of your heart.
And as you breathe in and breathe out, finding the brightness in that place.
And as you practice that way, if it doesn't seem bright, just keep gently trying.
And if, as might happen, you become flooded with the 10,000 ways in which you are not open hearted and generous, reflect that this is a wonderful thing.
Who is telling you that you're not open hearted and generous?
It's your open hearted generous heart that's telling you that.
Who else would know?
When you think about it, who else would know?
So appreciate that if it happens that way.
Or forget about all that and just practice in the way you're used to if you don't want to do all that.
I'm just trying to give you suggestions in case you're bored.
It's a long week, we're sitting here a lot, so you might need some suggestions.
So it's good that we, for whatever our reasons may be, have taken the time to clear our schedules, all the busy things that we have to do, to come here for a week, just to sit together in silence.
And I think we need to do this from time to time.
And we all know that, that's why we're here.
But it would be a mistake to think that the reason why we need to do this is that the world is a train wreck and it's hopeless, so we need to escape every now and then, otherwise we'll go crazy.
We might think like that, but this is not the case, I believe.
We may not yet know how to live in the world.
That's the problem, it's not the world.
And we're here not to escape so that we can go back and need to escape again later.
We're here because little by little by little we're all going to find a different way of living in the world, so that we realize that the world is not a train wreck.
It's not impossible.
If we know who we are, if we're not out of touch with the center of the Earth, we can live in peace and harmony no matter what the conditions are.
And when we learn how to do this, many people will benefit.
And we probably not, but practice goes on from the beginning of life to the end.
Retreat or no retreat, it's the same.
So again, thanks to everybody who's put in so much effort to make this possible.
And thanks to everyone here whose practice and sincere effort also is what it takes to create this for the rest of us.
